questions.prompt: In water, why do phospholipids form a bilayer instead of a single layer?

options.a: Heads face the water on both sides and tails hide in the middle
options.b: Tails face the water and heads hide in the middle
options.c: Heads clump together in the center of the membrane
options.d: Tails dissolve in water and form a single sheet

questions.prompt: Two membranes differ only in their fatty acid tails: one has saturated tails and one has unsaturated tails. Which is more fluid, and why?

options.a: Saturated, because its tails pack more tightly
options.b: Unsaturated, because double bends stop the tails from packing tightly
options.c: Saturated, because it has more double bonds
options.d: Both are equally fluid, because both have fatty acid tails

questions.prompt: Considering only the tail-packing effect described, which change explains membrane parts moving more freely?

options.a: More saturated tails, which pack closely and allow less movement.
options.b: More saturated tails, which pack loosely and allow more movement.
options.c: More unsaturated tails, which pack closely and allow less movement.
options.d: More unsaturated tails, which pack loosely and allow more movement.

questions.prompt: A student says cholesterol always makes a membrane more fluid. Which correction fits the explanation?

options.a: It limits movement in a very fluid membrane and promotes stiffening in the cold.
options.b: It increases movement in a very fluid membrane and prevents stiffening in the cold.
options.c: It limits movement in a very fluid membrane and prevents stiffening in the cold.
options.d: It increases movement in a very fluid membrane and promotes stiffening in the cold.

questions.prompt: A protein is seen moving sideways within a membrane made of lipids, cholesterol, and proteins. Which model describes this?

options.a: Bilayer model, which describes phospholipid heads facing water on both sides
options.b: Fluid mosaic model, which describes components that move within the membrane
options.c: Cholesterol buffer, which describes limiting movement when the membrane is too fluid
options.d: Glycocalyx, which describes a sugar coating that helps cells recognize each other

questions.prompt: Lipids rarely switch leaflets on their own. Which best explains lipids that do switch leaflets with help?

options.a: Special proteins such as flippases and scramblases help move them
options.b: Cholesterol pulls lipids across the membrane
options.c: Sugar chains on the outer surface carry lipids across
options.d: Lipids switch when their tails become saturated

questions.prompt: A student says the glycocalyx is inside the cell and mainly sets membrane fluidity. Which correction fits?

options.a: Inner surface, where it mainly sets membrane fluidity
options.b: Outer surface, where it mainly limits lipids flipping between leaflets
options.c: Outer surface, where it is a sugar coating that aids cell recognition
options.d: Inner surface, where it is made of phospholipid heads that stiffen membranes

questions.prompt: A student says fatty acid saturation is the only factor that affects membrane fluidity. Which correction fits?

options.a: Yes, saturation is the only factor affecting fluidity
options.b: No, chain length, temperature, and cholesterol also affect fluidity
options.c: No, fluidity depends only on the number of phospholipid heads
options.d: Yes, cholesterol alone determines all membrane fluidity

questions.prompt: A fatty acid tail has a double bond between two carbon atoms. What structure results?

options.a: A bend that stops the tail from packing tightly
options.b: A straight tail that packs tightly with its neighbors
options.c: A water-loving head that faces outward
options.d: A tail that is water-loving like a head

questions.prompt: Which statement about the two leaflets of a membrane is correct?

options.a: They have identical mixtures of molecules
options.b: Lipids often switch leaflets alone without help
options.c: Only proteins differ between the leaflets
options.d: They contain different mixtures of molecules

answer_key.rationale: Water-loving heads face water on both sides while water-avoiding tails hide in the middle, forming the bilayer.
Double bonds in unsaturated tails create bends that prevent tight packing, so those membranes are more fluid.
Unsaturated tails with double-bond bends pack loosely, letting membrane parts move more and increasing fluidity.
Cholesterol buffers fluidity: it limits movement when the membrane is too fluid and helps prevent stiffening when cold.
The fluid mosaic model describes a membrane mixing lipids, cholesterol, and proteins whose components can move sideways.
Flippases, floppases, and scramblases help lipids move between leaflets, since lipids rarely switch on their own.
The glycocalyx is a sugar coating from carbohydrate chains on the outer surface that aids cell recognition.
Fluidity is affected by fatty acid saturation, chain length, temperature, and cholesterol, not saturation alone.
A double bond creates a bend in an unsaturated tail, which stops the tails from packing tightly.
The two leaflets contain different mixtures of molecules, and lipids rarely switch leaflets without special protein help.
